subtopic: STATEMENT ON ARRANGEMENTS FOR FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON ARRANGEMENTS FOR FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement about arrangements in contemplation of the forthcoming constitutional conference which opens next Monday.
The agenda of the conference was included with my letter of January 16 to the provincial premiers, copies of which were tabled in the House of Commons on January 25 and included in Hansard of that day. In my letter I suggested to the premiers that "we agree to make public the opening sessions of the first day when the various governments ordinarily present their initial statements". I also suggested that consideration could be given to having the closing session public. Arrangements are accordingly being made to permit full coverage by television, radio and press for these sessions.
So far as admission to the conference room itself is concerned, the main problem is space. The conference will be held in room 200 of the west block. After providing for the various delegations and their staffs, for television and radio facilities, and for the translation and secretarial facilities that are necessary, there will, I am afraid, be very little space in the actual chamber itself for members of parliament, for representatives of the press or for others. It has seemed to the government to be best to divide what space there is equally between representatives of the information media and members of the different political parties represented in the House of Commons. I wrote yesterday to the leaders of the various parties indicating that there would be, of course, accommodation for the leaders themselves, and giving an allocation of seats on a
party basis roughly in proportion to representation in the house. It will be for each party to determine to what members the seats should be allocated.
For other members of parliament who may be in a position to be present and for the press we will have closed circuit television in a number of rooms in the west block. In addition there will be the normal television and radio facilities.
As I said yesterday, it will be for the conference to decide when and to what extent it may be desirable to hold executive sessions. Several of the premiers have expressed the view that executive sessions may be necessary for the purpose of negotiation and full and frank discussion leading to agreement. Such private sessions have, of course, been the almost invariable pattern, for federal-provincial conferences in the past, but I think a substantial departure from past practice is desirable because of the special nature and importance of the matters to be discussed.
As members are aware, the Minister of Justice is visiting the provincial capitals to have advance discussions with the premiers and their advisers in order to ensure that the meeting beginning February 5 will be as productive as possible. The government will also be publishing, and will table in the House of Commons later this week, a document on its proposal for the establishment of a Canadian charter of human rights. The recommendations of the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism have of course been public for some weeks and they will be on the agenda. I shall be making an opening statement to the conference, which I expect will be accompanied by additional material that will be made public-that is, the additional material -before the conference opens.
It is the hope of the government, as I am sure it is the hope of all members of the house, that we may see real progress at the conference itself and at meetings to follow, in the achievement of more satisfactory arrangements within the confederation of today and in the review of our constitution to ensure as effective provision as possible for the confederation of the future.

January 30, 1968

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON ARRANGEMENTS FOR FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the right hon. Prime Minister for his statement and the information he has given about the arrangements relating to the conference, in particular the arrangements made for representatives of parties in the house to attend as observers, as well as arrangements for other members of the house to follow the proceedings on closed circuit television.
The conference is, of course, one of tremendous importance. I would think it is certainly the most important federal-provincial conference to be held in my time in politics. It will certainly be the fervent wish of all members of the house, and indeed of all people in the country, that substantial progress be made.
The Prime Minister referred to a charter of human rights to be tabled in the house. We shall not attempt to make any comment on that until we see the proposed charter. If I may express a particular hope, however, it would be that it will be possible for the conference to make initial, substantial progress. I think we all recognize that the problems are of such an order that it would not be practical to expect a complete solution to be achieved in two or three days or even several times two or three days, but I hope the accomplishments in those two or three days will be substantial. I also hope that at the conference arrangements will be made for continuing not only discussion but working parties, so the country can proceed with actual work on these very important matters.
I repeat what I said when I started, that I regard this as a conference of the greatest importance and I wish the Prime Minister, his colleagues and the provincial premiers the utmost success in their deliberations.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON ARRANGEMENTS FOR FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are appreciative of the arrangements the Prime Minister has made so the various parties in this house can have representatives as observers at the proposed constitutional conference. I think this is a very useful move if the members of the house are to be properly informed so that later we can discuss intelligently the whole question of constitutional change in this country.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether he would give some thought to making it clear to the provincial premiers that if they in turn would like to include in their

delegations representatives from the opposition parties in the legislatures, they would be entitled to do so. I happen to know that in one or two instances premiers have indicated a willingness to do so, provided this were acceptable to the federal government. I think the more people we can involve in this dialogue that will go on for the next few months in Canada, the better the chance that we will get some mutual understanding of the problems.
I would also like to ask the Prime Minister whether he would give some thought to the possibility of the observers being allowed to sit through the closed sessions of the conference. I know this is not customary when federal-provincial conferences are discussing financial matters and agreements, but in view of the fact that at this exploratory conference matters will be discussed which will ultimately have to be debated in parliament and in all the provincial legislatures, it seems to me there would be a better opportunity for an understanding in depth of the problems that confront this country if the observers were allowed to attend throughout the entire conference. I recognize, of course, that the Prime Minister himself could not make this decision and that the premiers in attendance would also have to agree, but I would like to proffer it to the Prime Minister as a suggestion.
Finally I would urge again, as we have done so often in the past, that following this conference the Prime Minister give serious consideration to the setting up of a parliamentary committee to discuss the constitutional changes which may be necessary in this country to ensure that our constitution is in keeping with the times in which we live. The parliamentary committees which have been in operation during the past few years on a number of topics have demonstrated the extent to which it is possible in this house to achieve a consensus on many controversial subjects. I think a parliamentary committee might do the same thing with respect to constitutional changes.
I should like to say also that we consider this constitutional conference to be one of the most important gatherings in our time. We hope it will be a success, and certainly anything we can do to contribute to a better understanding and to better co-operation among all parts of Canada will be done to the fullest extent possible.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON ARRANGEMENTS FOR FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened to the statement made
January 30, 1968

by the Prime Minister and, for the time being, we are satisfied, though we will attend the conference as observers only, since I understand that representatives from every party will be invited.
I consider this conference as one of the most important ones up to now. We are entering in a negotiation era which will concern all the provinces and the whole country. I think that this conference greatly interests all the parties in the house.
We bitterly regret that our parliamentary system does not allow representatives of the opposition to participate actively in the negotiations instead of attending the conference only as observers. Having been elected by the people, I feel that we are all equal and that we have the same responsibilities. I have always deplored the fact that, in such a case as this, we attend simply as observers while the party in power negotiates the agreements. To my mind, this is a defect in our parliamentary system.
I should like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister and, indirectly, the premiers of all provinces, to look into the possibility of inviting us to the negotiating table in this most important circumstance for the whole of the country.
We will consider it a pleasure and a duty to appoint a representative of our party as an observer to follow the progress of this conference which, I hope, will suggest a constitution more beneficial to all provinces and more likely to contribute further to unite Canada from coast to coast.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)

subtopic: STATEMENT ON ARRANGEMENTS FOR FORTHCOMING CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we would like to thank the Prime Minister for the outline he has given us today with respect to the forthcoming federal-provincial conference. I think it is logical to give the members of this house the opportunity of attending the conference, at least as observers, because in recent months some criticism has been voiced over the fact that we seemed to be moving in the direction of government by federal-provincial conference. I believe this move will assist in dispelling the fears in this direction.
The Prime Minister has indicated something of the agenda for the conference. I was rather perturbed to read in the newspapers the other day a statement to the effect that an outline of the government's proposals to be advanced at the conference was presented to
Inquiries of the Ministry the Quebec Liberal convention. I thought this was rather improper, if such was the case, and perhaps there should be some clarification of this point.
I am sure we all desire the further development of our confederation. Without question there will be a wide divergence of opinion as to how this objective is to be achieved. As has been stated, this conference will be more or less of an exploratory nature and it will take a great deal more discussion and many more conferences to work out a program that will be adequate for the needs of Canada and contribute to the development of this great nation.

On clause 2-Broadcasting policy for Canada.

Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned last night, I was stating my opposition to the passing of clause 2(i) of Bill No. C-163.
I was saying that education is not a matter of federal responsibility but that, under the British North America Act, it comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces. That is why I do not see any need for paragraph (i) which stipulates that:
-facilities should be provided within the Canadian broadcasting system for educational broadcasting.
I was saying, Mr. Chairman, that Quebec already has facilities for educational broadcasting and I would like to correct my statement to that effect. It would have been more

January 30, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting accurate to say that Quebec owns a studio and that it has rented some equipment to make films that would be shown on television as educational programs.
In fact, there is now a pilot project known as "Tevec" which is merely an experiment, as should be done normally. A quite numerous team is now working on this.
A series of studio programs has been produced with rented equipment, it is true, and not only is the project under way, but it is making good progress.
A few members of that team were telling me today that if the experiment proved a success, Quebec would purchase equipment for educational broadcasting and if it failed, it would drop the project. Therefore, I am of the opinion that it is useless to provide the Canadian broadcasting system with such equipment which will be of no use, since experiments would have been unsuccessful.
Therefore, I wonder why that subclause is included in Bill No. C-163. I think that it would be a duplicate use of public funds, since Quebec is now organizing such an educational broadcasting system, since it already has a well-experienced team working in that field and has rented the complete equipment to start producing educational programs. I wonder why Ottawa would start over and pay again for present facilities.
Administrative efficiency requires indeed that duplication of expenses be avoided for already available equipment.
This is why, Mr. Chairman, as a result of the constitutional and practical arguments which I put forward yesterday in affecting to that subclause, the presentation of an amendment is advisable.
Therefore, I would move that subclause (i) of clause 2 be purely and simply deleted, because it adds nothing to the bill on Canadian broadcasting and, moreover, it is contrary to the constitution, to the British North America Act.
If the hon. member is against this subclause of clause 2, all he has to do to show his disapproval is to vote against it when it is put to the vote.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want this part in respect of educational facilities to pass without making some remarks about it. When the committee on broadcasting begins 

its hearings on educational television one of the problems it will have to solve is the definition of educational television. I suggest it might be a little difficult to define this phrase because there are two possible definitions. The first relates to educational television for elementary and secondary schools and perhaps colleges. The second relates to adult education.
Having regard to school broadcasting, it seems to me there has been an inexcusable delay in bringing in a bill to establish facilities for educational television. At least two provinces that I know of, Alberta and Ontario, have been pressing the federal government for some time to build these transmission facilities. Indeed, Alberta was ready to start a year and a half ago and Ontario has been rather impatient.
The committee on broadcasting is going to begin its hearings on this subject on February 8. It will be hearing from those provinces which wish to be represented and from representatives of private organizations and perhaps from individuals. At the rate we are dealing with broadcasting matters here in Ottawa it is difficult to tell when this program will actually come into force. The committee will hold hearings in February and March and some time after that the bill will come back to the house. So educational broadcasting may not even begin in the year 1968.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I have the feeling so far as school broadcasting is concerned that we are once again in the position where events may overtake us. It seems to me that before very long schools in the urban areas of Canada will not be requiring the regular, through the air transmission facilities. With the developments which have taken taken place in closed circuit systems, more extensive use of films and videotapes and that sort of thing, it seems to me that the larger centres and any school district which is in an urban area will not need through the air facilities. They may still be required for some time to come in rural areas, but I suggest that technical developments are overtaking us in this field.
With regard to the second possible definition of educational television, that concerning adult education, I think there are some difficulties. The definition is very difficult. "Adult education" can mean almost anything, It can mean the ordinary type of public affairs broadcasting which is now taking

place on the regular television and radio stations, it can mean actual instruction in university and college courses tor adults, and it can mean instruction of the type with which the department of manpower is concerned. I remind the hon. member for Lapointe that this is a very legitimate concern of the federal government which recognizes that it is responsible for manpower training. Mr. Chairman, it is my intention to move an amendment to this subclause. Without speaking at tedious length on the reasons therefor, I thank the minister for having stood this clause yesterday and giving me an opportunity to speak to the clause and move my amendment today. I told the committee that I intended to move an amendment
January 30, 1968	COMMONS
to this subclause because I am unhappy with the authoritarian and arbitrary type of permanent decision the present wording would seem to make where disputes between private broadcasters and the national service, the C.B.C., are concerned. My amendment is:
That In subclause (h) of clause 2 all the words after the word "system" be struck out, and the following substituted therefor: "the public interest must prevail".
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the subclause, if amended along the lines I have suggested, would read as follows:
(h) where any conflict arises between the objectives of the national broadcasting service and the interests of the private element of the Canadian broadcasting system, the public interest must prevail.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
My reasons for suggesting this amendment were expressed in the debate on December 21 and I have made reference to them on the two or three occasions when I have spoken during the clause by clause examination of the legislation in the past week and a half. My reasons are that the clause as worded at the present time lays down a rigid, codified decision of a permanent nature from which there is no appeal and no escape. I envision a situation where possibly two, three or four years from now, some time in the future when all the innuendoes and philosophizing in this debate have been concluded, when the legislation is written into the statute books and becomes the code under which the broadcasting authorities, administrators and operators in this country carry out their function, a dispute might arise over a given broadcasting prize, whether it be a channel, a frequency, a type of program or an event available for transmission. In such a case the authority- the B.B.G. or the Canadian television commission as it may become known-would have one firm guide line under which to act and there would be no opportunity for the private operator to have his case fairly heard.
I say that because I think any honest and conscientious examination of the wording will lead all hon. members to the same conclusion. On looking at these words one finds that the proposed legislation stipulates that where any conflict arises between the objectives of the national broadcasting service, that is, the C.B.C., and the interests of the private element of the Canadian broadcasting system, the objectives of the national broadcasting service must prevail. These objectives can cover a wide variety of interests, plans, hopes, dreams and aspirations.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
The word "objectives" is most ambiguous, far reaching and all embracing. It is open to many interpretations. It is possible, as I suggested, that the objective of the C.B.C. might be to obtain a certain channel, frequency or access to the coverage of an event. I believe that this type of objective was not envisaged by those who drafted the legislation. The framers of the legislation and those of us who were exposed to the wording in the standing committee on broadcasting had a more abstract and perhaps a more esoteric idea of the objectives. But the fact is that in the harsh light of dawn and under the harsh light of examination by members of this committee the term as it stands in the proposed legislation is fraught with difficulties and dangers so far as the freedom of the Canadian society in the future is concerned.
The amendment I propose eliminates the danger of authoritarian permanency which is contained in the original wording and provides that where such a conflict arises the public interest must prevail. I suggest that this in an entirely acceptable position to all members of the house regardless of their political persuasion, regardless of their partisanship on the question of broadcasting, and regardless of whether they favour public over private broadcasting or vice-versa. It is the public interest that is important, not the interests of the national broadcasting service or its objectives, nor the interests of private broadcasters or their objectives.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave):
That in subclause (h) of clause 2 all the words after the word "system" be struck out, and the following substituted therefor: "the public interest must prevail;"

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word or two on this amendment. I agree substantially with what the hon. member for Winnipeg South has said. There are two other words in the clause that I do not like. I do not like the word "objectives" in so far as it relates to the national broadcasting service, the C.B.C., and I do not like the word "interests" in so far as it is applied to the private sector. My reason for saying that is that the clause as it stands says in effect that the C.B.C. will always have its way and that the will of the C.B.C. will always prevail. In the clause as it now stands we are comparing objectives on the one hand and interests on the other. Surely we should be comparing
January 30, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting objectives with objectives, or interests with interests, and not clothing the plans of the C.B.C. in the best possible raiment by using the word "objectives" and downgrading the plans and intentions of the private sector by calling them merely "interests".
We have been told that the broadcasting system in Canada is made up of two substantial sectors, the public sector and the private sector, and that both are in many ways equally important. My understanding is that in terms of capital investment or employment they are comparable in size and are doing a comparable job for the country. Therefore in this respect both merit consideration. In other words, the terms of reference given to the over-all broadcasting authority which should arbitrate between them should a conflict arise should not be such as to load the dice heavily in favour of one sector. I suggest that under the present wording the dice are heavily loaded in favour of the national broadcasting service.
I suggest also that the clause as it stands downgrades the powers of the over-all regulatory authority. If the objectives of the national broadcasting service must always prevail against the private interests, then surely many cases can be settled out of court without any argument. Surely the C.B.C. will have little difficulty in proving its case. All it needs to say is that its plans are consistent with its objectives and then in effect it is home free. Rarely will it say that its plans are in fact in conflict with its objectives.
I can imagine cases such as the following. Let us assume that the C.T.Y. network has lined up the Grey cup game, as I believe it has in fact done for the next period of years in a contractual arrangement with the Canadian football league, and the national broadcasting service comes along as it did some years back, and says that it wants a piece of the Grey cup broadcast. All it needs to do is to point to one of those wonderful objectives which are outlined in subclause (g), that of covering most or all of Canada, and it is home free.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Its objective of covering all of Canada is consistent with its plan to get the Grey cup broadcast, or vice-versa. This plan is consistent with one of these great objectives.
I would much rather see this clause provide that when there is a conflict between the national broadcasting service and the private sector the issue be resolved by the over-all

authority and that the criteria be the public interest. I do not like the word "objectives" and I do not like the word "interests". I do not like the way one is attached to the national broadcasting service and the other to the private sector to the detriment of the latter. concluding paragraph of the report on the white paper on broadcasting, over the signature of the hon. member of York-Scarbor-ough, presented on March 21, 1967, reads:

His first wife was named Matilda and she died and was buried. When the old man was dying he was asked about the place of his burial. His second wife's name was Bertha. The old man said, ''When I die, bury me between Matilda and Bertha". He thought for a while and then he said, "Tilt me a little toward Bertha". It seems to me that really is what parliament wants us to do. If there is a primacy as between the private and public sectors, parliament feels it should be given to the instrument of the people of Canada in broadcasting, the public sector.
This clause does not say, nor is it intended to say, that when the interests of the private sector are opposed to the interests of the public sector the interests of the public sector shall hold sway. If it said that I would agree with hon. members that it would intend that the C.B.C., whenever it came into conflict with private broadcasters, must win. This is not the case. It is the objectives this parliament has laid down which must be paramount. Otherwise you would have a situation where the B.B.G., or whatever the new regulatory body is, would be put in the position that it would have to try to hold the C.B.C. paramount over the interests of the private broadcasters. I do not believe anyone really means to argue that.
I cannot, therefore, agree with the amendment which is offered nor with those who support it from this side. I should like to say that it is quite clear what would happen if you oppose interests and interests, but you must realize that is not what is being done here. That means the C.B.C.

-of the Canadian broadcasting system, the objectives of the national broadcasting service must prevail;

For example, in the transportation field we have the state-owned Canadian National Railways and the privately owned Canadian Pacific Railway. Yet this is what we seem to be saying in this subclause. At any rate, it might be interpreted in that way.

Does it mean the objectives of the C.B.C. as set out in subclause (g) of clause 2? If so, why does it not say so? During the course of this rather long debate many members have expressed concern about the type of programs that the C.B.C. has provided from time to time in the past. Personally I am inclined to think that their concern is not soundly based. I believe that the days of a free-wheeling C.B.C. are clearly over. The debate that has taken place in this house indicates that the free-wheeling C.B.C. of the past is dead and that in the future a much greater danger is that the C.B.C. will become the strong right arm of the state, with all the forebodings that that implies. Bolstered by large public revenues, immune from control by parliament, the C.B.C. could become in the future a danger to the public interest rather than a supporter of the public interest. In these circumstances the suggestion that this subclause should be amended in order to provide that where there is a conflict between the state-owned C.B.C. and the privately owned stations it should be resolved in the public interest should commend itself to members on this side of the house as well as to opposition members.
I urge the minister to reconsider the possibility of moving a very simple amendment to clarify, first, the meaning of the word "objectives" and, second, to make it entirely clear that there is to be no automatic resolution of any conflict in favour of the state-owned system but rather that the public interest will be the governing factor.

Mr. Chairman, I thought I had made it perfectly clear that the latter was the case and also that the objectives were those in subclause (g) and those preceding it. It is very clear that these are the objectives that parliament has set for its servants.

Mr. Chairman, I support the amendment moved by my colleague. I went to the table and borrowed The Concise Oxford Dictionary in order to determine the difference between the word "objectives" and the word "interests". The minister is quite right when she says there is a difference in meaning, but I suggest that it is more a dictionary difference than one that has practical application here. The word "interest" in the particular context under debate means "Thing in which one is concerned", according to The Concise Oxford Dictionary. "Objective" means a "point aimed at".
In the practical context under discussion it is almost impossible to distinguish between what is an objective of the C.B.C. and what is an interest of the private element. This would

certainly be the case if both were to become engaged in a dispute about, for example, the issuance of a licence or who should carry the Grey cup broadcast or the like. I think that any lawyer who was trying to interpret this subclause would do his darndest to see that the point in dispute became an objective of the C.B.C. and an interest of the private element. In the event of a conflict-and the bill does say "where any conflict arises"-if he could label what the C.B.C. was after as an objective and what the private element was after as an interest he would have won the battle. It will not be served by giving the right to build a station to the C.B.C., which may not have the money to do so for years and years and years, but by giving the right to erect a station to those who can make that station available immediately. I hope the minister will reconsider the matter and accept what I think is a sensible amendment.

Before the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond interjects with his pointed remarks, to meet the point which has been raised, perhaps the amendment might be changed to read something like, "where any conflict arises between the public interest as determined by the objectives of the national broadcasting service and the interests of the private element of the Canadian broadcasting system, the public interest must prevail." In other words, that would pretty well define the public interest as being the objective here.
Is the minister suggesting that the words, "the public interest must prevail", should be inserted in the amendment?

I was suggesting that the wording should be, "where any conflict arises between the public interest as determined by the objectives of the national broadcasting service", and so on, and that the last phrase on line 35 should be, "the public interest must prevail". I do not ask for comment now but I think we should think about this while listening to the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond.

Mr. Chairman, the words of the subclause were inspired by a member of the Progressive Conservative party, the hon. member for Royal. As a member of the steering committee I can remember that the language of the subclause was largely inspired as a result of the work performed by the hon. member for Royal. I agreed with him and applauded him for the wording which he suggested in the steering committee. I am sorry he is not here today because no doubt he would make a statement defending the words which he suggested in the first place.
I agree with the Secretary of State that there should be tilt in favour of the public system. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano said that private and public broadcasting in Canada are equally important. They are not
January 30, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting equally important so far as parliament is concerned, and that is evident from the bill.
In this bill clause 2(g) imposes a special responsibility on the national broadcasting service. If some of the arguments that have been put forward were adopted we would in fact be running counter to some of the arguments for national unity. That is a special charge imposed on the national broadcasting service. It must also extend broadcasting services to all parts of Canada, as clause 2 suggests, even where that may not be profitable. No one blames private broadcasters for not establishing stations where there is no market. But people in all parts of Canada should receive broadcasting services, whether or not those services are profitable, and in this bill we are talking about providing such a national broadcasting service in both langauges.
I am sure the hon. member for York-Humber will say there is no apparent market in Toronto for French broadcasting. The same holds true for Vancouver because there is no market there for a French station. Even though there is no market in the commercial sense, the public broadcasting service will extend its service to those areas. Through subclause (g) the national service is charged with a special responsibility to express the Canadian identity and to attempt to forge national unity. It seems to me clear that Mr. R. B. Bennett, in planning the public broadcasting service, intended that service to be the predominant service in the country. Parliament expects that service to be predominant. Almost every national organization, including the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian Association of Consumers, has expressed this view when they have appeared before the broadcasting committee.
I take issue with what the hon. member for Winnipeg South suggests. There is nothing rigid about this provision. This clause is a preamble and declaration and I doubt that every word in it could be enforced in a court of law. Nevertheless it is a declaration of parliament and I think the wording should stand. I again remind members of the official opposition that it was their chief broadcasting critic, the hon. member for Royal, who moved the adoption of the wording we have now.

Mr. Chairman, I must say that I found the lady minister's humour more acceptable than the change she suggested
[Mr. Prittie.l
with regard to the point brought to the committee's attention by the hon. member for Winnipeg South and amplified by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano.
You did not laugh.

No, but I smiled. I did not write down the suggested change, but I do not think the wording corrects the situation. At first blush it appears to make it worse because you are defining the public interest and including words such as "shall be the objective of the national broadcasting service". It surprises me, as it has surprised many others here, that a government labelled as Liberal should advocate such a clause as this which is perhaps one of the most invidious in the bill in that as drafted it says that any conflict between public and private broadcasters shall be resolved in favour of the national broadcasting service.
I am also amazed that members of the N.D.P. should think the words and actions of Mr. R. B. Bennett are sacrosanct. Undoubtedly in the 1930's, when the national broadcasting service was radio only, the setting up of such a service was a tremendous accomplishment. The service has performed well. I have always been amazed that members to the left who profess to be so progressive, so go-go, so up to date with everything, whose ranks are joined in ever-increasing numbers by columnists and commentators who want to participate in politics, should go back to the thirties in their thinking and imagine that the thinking of the thirties can provide a cure for today and the future.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond in his usual way drew a red herring across our arguments. He said in effect that this clause contains only terms of reference. All I can say to that is that we have spent several days discussing these terms of reference. As the minister has said, this clause is the heart of the bill. Clause 2 is the guts of the bill, and while the subclause we are now considering, when passed, may not have the force of law, it certainly will contain terms of reference which will guide the new council.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
As the hon. member for Halifax suggested, there can be a considerable difference between one's interest and one's objective. Take the case of the unfortunate gentleman -perhaps fortunate, depending on how one views the state of matrimony-who had two wives. His objective was to be buried
January 30, 1968

between the two ladies. That was his objective. But he had an interest in being tilted toward one rather than the other. There is no doubt that the gentleman wanted to be buried between the two ladies, but he had a little more interest in one of them.
But what was his objective?
His objective was to be buried. Any activity after that was pretty Sterile.
Then surely the hon. member realizes that his interest and his objective were the same.

Let us say that any amorous objective had long ceased and expired.
Be that as it may, the story does illustrate the difficulty in trying to define an interest as apart from an objective. One could have an objective and at the same time have an interest which pursued that objective, but I do not know whether the reverse cannot be true. It occasionally happens that a phrase in French cannot be transcribed into English because of semantic difficulties. Here, in the English language, we find a paragraph which can only add to the difficulties of the council in any attempt it may make to distinguish between interest and objective, no matter what semblance of plausibility the minister may appear to give to the clause.
This is a key clause. The position taken by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, with all his eloquence and sincerity, confirms our belief that this is a fundamental concept. It does not matter greatly who drafted the provision or what has taken place since the committee hearings. I am completely opposed to a clause which, without further ado, would resolve matters completely in favour of the C.B.C. Even if the committee accepted the plausible explanation given by the minister in defining "interest" and "objective", the provisions as set out are so general as to encourage the council to decide automatically in favour of the pubic network.
We have gone far beyond Mr. Bennett and the thirties. For example, we have developed a modern transportation service, as the hon. member for St. Paul mentioned. Let us go out west to the region the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond comes from. No doubt he would tell us he would like to see one state-owned air service in Canada. Fortunately, not very long ago we had a progressive
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting government which did something about public transportation in the air and developed competition between Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines. I should like to hear the hon. members for Burnaby-Richmond, Burna-by-Coquitlam and New Westminster, who all come from the beautiful province of British Columbia where I was fortunate enough to practice law for several years, say in this house today that they do not like this development or that it has is not helped to improve Air Canada service as well as provide better service for the public.
And provide the biggest payrolls in British Columbia.

That is so. I know that birds flock to Victoria to a far greater extent than they do to Ottawa, but in any event I doubt that there is any wish to revert to the old transportation system and allow all questions to be resolved in favour of Air Canada. If this had been done there would today be no alternative air service over the Rocky Mountains.
As I say, we have advanced beyond the thirties. I was somewhat disappointed to hear the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond reverting to the thirties for his argument and trying to keep us in that period when we have progressed beyond it, notably with regard to the affairs of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. We have established the Canadian Transport Commission to resolve conflicts. Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines now supply alternative services, with the Canadian Transport Commission or the Air Transport Board ready to resolve differences.
Why, then, should there be so much hesitation about writing into the bill a provision such as we are suggesting? As things stand, with the prestige of the C.B.C. and the weight of public money flowing into that organization there would have to be a very strong case indeed before the council would fail to resolve in favour of the C.B.C. I say the effect will be to castrate the council. Why give powers to the council as is done under clause 16 unless room is given for the exercise of those powers and the reaching of a fair determination when conflicts arise?
For these reasons and many more which I could advance I hope the minister will reconsider the position she has taken. The amendments advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg South might, in my opinion, have included a few words to make it clearly

January 30, 1968
Private Bills
understood that when conflict does arise between the national system and the private system the interest of the public should prevail. I see nothing archaic or antediluvian about this or any bar to its adoption by the government which prides itself on traditional forms of Liberal philosophy. I think I shall now call it six o'clock.

Would the hon. member answer one question? I was sad to hear him say he was distressed by reference to the late R. B. Bennett. Has he made such violent objection on every occasion when his former leader went back a hundred years or so to Sir John Macdonald?

The hon. lady cannot have heard me in many debates because today I was not really violent at all. My voice was just going up and down. It was simply that I was disappointed in the approach of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond.

[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
The house resumed, from Tuesday, November 7, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-105, to incorporate Rainbow Pipe Line Corporation-Mr. Orange-Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee rose on Tuesday, November 7, clause 1 of the bill was under consideration. Shall clause 1 carry?
On clause 1-Incorporation.

Mr. Chairman, as you have
said, this matter was given some consideration on November 7. Some time last June the committee of the whole house also considered the bill and it had, of course, been dealt with somewhat extensively, though not as extensively as some of us would have liked, in the standing committee on transport and communications.
If one looks in a cursory way at the debate in committee of the whole it will be found that there has been a considerable amount of opposition and adverse speculation concerning the intent and purpose of this company. The speculation and opposition and the doubts about the company and the operation of the pipe line itself stem from all parties in the house. Therefore the concern in regard to this company has not been narrow or partisan but rather pretty broad and general.
I do not, of course, wish to put the hon. member for the Northwest Territories in an awkward position in respect of this bill, but quite frankly the fact that the proceedings with regard to the bill have been delayed from time to time indicates to me that even the sponsor of the bill had some doubts about its merits and what the operations of this company might be. One has only to look at the number of times the bill has been called to be proceeded with and then has been permitted to stand.
My hon. friend holds up a finger to indicate that this occurred once. It occurred last Thursday as well and on other occasions prior to the bill being given second reading. If I am mistaken I stand corrected and apologize to the hon. member for the Northwest Territories. However, this is my understanding from watching the proceedings in respect of this bill. My understanding is that it has not been proceeded with on several occasions when called by the Chair. We all know that when this happens with regard to a private bill it simply means either that the sponsor is not in possession of all the information he would like to have about the structure of the operation of the company or that he has some doubts about it which need to be resolved in his own mind.
Because a number of objections and doubts have been expressed by members in the
January 30, 1968

house and in committee concerning the bill I am quite sure the officers and agents of the company, not to mention the hon. member for the Northwest Territories, have looked at these objections and doubts and are perhaps prepared to try to allay the doubts and fears expressed by hon. members. It may be that at some subsequent stage of the bill the hon. member for the Northwest Territories may have some comments to make concerning the doubts that have been expressed in the past. He may not have that opportunity today, incidentally, and whether the opportunity will arise on some subsequent Thursday is problematical. However, as long as the doubts which have been expressed by members on both sides of the house remain I think it behoves us not to pass the bill until they are cleared up. This matter will be explored later by some of my colleagues.
One aspect of the bill that concerns me is one which has concerned me in respect of other companies that have come before us during this hour to seek authorization. I refer to the ownership, control and authority behind the particular company. This is set out on page 7 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on transport and communications for June 20 last. Mr. Barroll, vice president of Mobil Oil Canada Limited, pointed out that the ownership of Rainbow Pipe Line Corporation was fairly well equally controlled by three major oil companies. He lists the ownership. He states that Imperial Oil Limited has a 33J per cent equity, that Mobil Oil Canada Limited has a 33 J per cent equity, that Ac-quitaine Canada Limited has a 30 per cent equity and that Banff Oil Limited has a 3J per cent interest. Later there was some mention of the possibility that Acquitaine Canada Limited owned and controlled Banff Oil and that if that were the case the ownership, either directly or indirectly, was equally shared among Imperial Oil Limited, Mobil Oil Canada Limited and Acquitaine Canada Limited.
As I understand it, not one of these parent companies is a Canadian company in the sense that it is owned and controlled in Canada, even though the bill says that not less than two-thirds of the directors of Rainbow shall, at all times, be persons resident in Canada and Canadian citizens. I submit that this would not detract from the degree of foreign ownership which, incidentally, is 100 per cent. In this case, as I believe we have proposed on other occasions with regard to
Private Bills
insurance companies, I think there should be an element of Canadianism involved and that we should develop some wording-and I believe there is ample precedent for such wording to be used-which we could insert in the bill to indicate that parliament will give the company a reasonable period of time in the future to divest itself of its foreign ownership and complexion and become Canadian owned and controlled. In fact this is one aspect which I think should be cleared out of the way before we proceed to give final passage to the bill.
Another point about which I am concerned, and about which I expressed some thoughts on another occasion, Involves the export of raw materials. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development not many months ago, although I cannot from memory either quote the words or cite the occasion, propounded fairly strongly the concept that particularly in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory we should bend every effort to develop the resources in the area. In other words, we should try to process in the territories whatever resource it may be through the various steps to the final manufactured or finished product. I am sure the hon. member for Northwest Territories, the sponsor of the bill, supports that principle. We all do because we are thinking in terms of Canadianism and the parochial necessity to develop industries close to the source of the raw material. This is true because such development provides the greatest amount of economic wealth to the area, e (6:10 p.m.)
As one of the objectives of the bill the company intends to export the raw material not only from the Northwest Territories to other parts of Canada but also out of the country. Information in this regard was given to the committee. Mr. Barroll, vice president of Mobil Oil, said the following, as recorded on page 3 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on transport and communications for Tuesday, June 20 last:
If you will permit me, I might make a statement here as to the location of the Rainbow Pipe Line system relative to the major crude oil distribution systems that exist in Canada today.
Apparently they had a map, although I did not see it, not being a member of the committee. Presumably this was pointed out to the members. He then said:
As shown on this map Rainbow Pipe Line system, as it is currently constructed, some 478 miles to this point here, connects to the terminals of Trans

Januaiy 30. 1968
Private Bills
Mountain Pipe Line and Interprovincial Pipe Line. These are the main trunk line systems that supply crude oil to the west coast refineries and the general export area here on the northeast coast of Washington.
If this company ever gets into operation, part of its proposal is to connect producing crude wells in the Northwest Territories with export systems which eventually reach the northwestern United States. Mr. Barroll then went on to say, as recorded on the same page:
In addition, of course, the system ties into the Interprovincial system which extends down through the United States to eastern Canada and supplies the important prairie markets and the markets in the Great Lakes area and, of course, the Sarnia market which is the principal destination for this crude.
The primary purpose of this company is to get the crude out of the Northwest Territories and to the Sarnia market. Mr. Barroll then talks about the desire of the company to enter the Chicago market which, at least at that time, was a relatively short crude oil area, as he put it.
I suggest that we should explore this whole matter thoroughly because we are apparently being asked to express a lack of concern for the well-being of the economy of the Northwest Territories in which this field exists. We are being asked to allow the extraction of crude oil from the Northwest Territories. Crude oil in its original state is of small value because it has received only the smallest amount of processing. As a raw material is processed its value increases. We are being asked, by allowing the export of this raw material, to disregard the potential interests of the people of the Northwest Territories. This is contrary to what the minister responsible for Indian affairs has suggested in respect of the national resources of these areas. We should not take the raw materials out of these areas before processing because this results in the lowest revenue for the people at the source. Surely that is not good in terms of Canadianism.
I am also disturbed by the requested powers and authority for this company. It has been said that the Rainbow Pipe Line Company is looking merely for a hunting licence. The company apparently wants to be placed in a monopoly position in order that it may do whatever it likes with the resources of this area, but let me remind hon. members that such a monopoly position puts everybody else in a disadvantageous position.

Let me refer again to the proceedings of the committee to indicate the philosophy inherent in the promotions of this company. Mr. Barroll said, as recorded on page 9, after quite extensive explanation about other aspects:
As a matter of prudence the solicitors for, and the management of, Rainbow Pipe Line Company deemed it advisable to get powers as broad as this committee saw fit to grant, so that they would be in a position to move into any area of transportation through pipe lines.
In other words, the company was saying, let us get everything we can. We may never need what we get but let us have the right to do sundry things. This company is seeking the right, without restriction or confinement, to do a variety of things. By way of comparison I think it is reasonable at this stage to refer to the bill which was being considered by the house earlier today. That bill would provide authority to a corporation to operate radio stations, microwave systems, television stations, interstation radio communication facilities, teletype, telephones and heaven only knows what else in the field of communications without restriction and without regard to whether or not the activity of that corporation is in the best interests of the country or the people of Canada. That corporation seeks authority in blanket form from the parliament of Canada to own, lease, operate and maintain all these facilities subject to the regulations and provisions of the Radio Act or any other statute relating to such communications facilities.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
In almost every case which has come to our attention of a company seeking authority such as this the officers of that company have had the grace to say they only want such authority and power for the purpose of carrying out its business activities. The company named in the bill before us suggests that its solicitors and management feel it prudent, in Mr. Bar-roll's own words, to obtain the broadest powers possible. So they even, and I submit they did it deliberately, excluded the normal saving words in such a clause restricting the company particularly to its own undertaking. Of course, sundry other rights are asked for in the bill, including permission to carry out various activities such as the maintenance and operation of aircraft and aerodromes-In this instance they point out that this activity is for the purpose of the company's undertaking-together with all the facilities and
January 30, 1968

appurtenances that go along with the operation of aircraft and aerodromes.
Now I come to the hunting licence aspect of the bill. The company seeks the right to search and prospect for gas, oil and other hydrocarbons and related substances or any of them, the right to drill for, extract and produce, store, refine, process, purchase, transport and distribute natural and artificial gas, oil and so on and, in fact, to do whatever other things oil companies do with respect to their search activities.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I must advise the hon. member that the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Chairman, we had before us the other day a bill that contained the same type of garbage about which the hon. member for Skeena has been speaking. In that case the company decided that there obviously had to be some compromise between its hope to operate a pipe line and the lawyers' hope to have everything but the kitchen sink included in the bill. The company thought it would be wise to present a bill which would enable it to operate as a pipe line rather than presenting one that had no chance of passing. Therefore they compromised to the extent of presenting a bill asking for permission to operate a pipe line.
It is my opinion that the fault does not lie only with the lawyers who advise pipe line companies. Certainly I am not presuming to tell Imperial Oil whom it should hire as lawyers. I think some of the fault lies with the Senate. I believe that the legislation it is providing as a model for pipe line companies is a disgrace to that august body, and it is legislation that we certainly do not intend to endorse. The sooner the other place is advised that a company coming before parliament should ask only for what it wants, the better chance that company will have of receiving permission to do those things. Companies that ask for many things they do not really want but which they presume there might be a faint possibility of using 50 years later had better ask for those things when they are wanted and members of parliament will consider them. A good example is this bill and several earlier pipe line bills.
For the last few days we have been discussing the Broadcasting Act. We will be creating in effect a new television and radio communications system. That bill deals with
Private Bills
satellites, radar towers and all the other paraphernalia that go with communications systems.
To be fair to the pipe line companies, many of them have very sophisticated communications systems which are necessary for their operations and to enable them to keep in communication with stations along the line. But when they present legislation to us such as that contained in this bill I say it is a disgrace for members of parliament to vote for it. This is especially so when the company has told the committee that it has no intention of using some of the powers for which it is asking. Yet we allow such bills to pass because some lawyer in a fantasy thinks it is a service or function that might be useful at some time and it is therefore included in the bill.
I am interested in this bill for two reasons. I believe that before the bill passes the garbage should be removed from it. I think that will be done if the company sincerely wants to operate a pipe line. In that event they will ask for permission to operate a pipe line and will present a bill which will enable them to do so. They will not ask for permission to operate a communications system or systems, the right to own houses, distribute power and do the many other things included in the bill.
The other problem is much more important. It involves a discussion we had with several people concerning a bill that was passed previously. That bill was in the same field as this and provided somewhat the same coverage. I would like to refer to the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on transport and communications of June 20 last and the evidence of Mr. Bar-roll. The company made a presentation to the committee and Mr. Barroll, the vice president of Mobil Oil, gave evidence before the committee. The seventh point in the conclusions he presented to the committee was as follows:
Finally, the people of Canada have a direct financial interest in development of petroleum resources in federally administered territories. It is to the advantage of Canada, we believe, to pass enabling legislation permitting the development of these resources so as to accelerate return to the government of Canada of royalty and lease sale revenue.
I agree with this. I also think that we have to decide for ourselves whether it is advantageous. We have to decide whether what we are doing is to the advantage of Canada or to the advantage of the oil company concerned. This company makes no bones about the fact

will never produce or people who are settling in an area which might not turn out to be as profitable as they had hoped.
When we set up the National Energy Board we stated that it should look after some of our responsibilities in this field. Frankly I do not think they are doing a good job in the south because they have allowed everything to go to the United States, to the extent that the Americans are now complaining about the export of our natural resources in the field of petroleum. We have not asked the National Energy Board whether it is necessary for 10 common carriers to go into the Northwest Territories, where as yet no oil is being produced, apart from Norman Wells and several other small developments. I exclude Norman Wells because there is a refinery there, but it is the only producer in the area. Yet we have now granted one charter and we are being asked to grant another. I believe that in the next two or three years we might be asked to grant five or six others. I ask hon. members: Why have we not called the National Energy Board before us in connection with these bills and asked some of their experts to give us a projection of the need for petroleum in the Northwest Territories? This is not a provincial matter, but one which is the responsibility of the federal government. We are acting both as a pseudo provincial government and as the federal government, and therefore we have a double responsibility in this field.
I think hon. members are either heing unfair to themselves or stupid, and I suggest it is not the latter. The situation in which we find ourselves is partly due to the way in which these bills are presented and partly to the unfairness of the committee structure and the way in which we operate, which does not allow us to provide the necessary protection. We have not called on the National Energy Board to come before the committee and make its recommendations. I should like to see the sponsor of the bill ask that the bill be returned to the committee for further study and that the National Energy Board be requested to provide us with some information with regard to the necessary protection. I note the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway, through the Vawn Pipe Line and the Rainbow Pipe Line, have explored the area and have found there is not enough crude for both of them, and that in fact there will not be enough crude for either of them if the potential is not there. I was advised that this was the situation so far as
Private Bills
the Rainbow Pipe Line is concerned and that the three lines which are now going out of the Rainbow field into Edmonton have a greater capacity than is justified. This field did not turn out quite as well as was anticipated.
These matters should be considered by members of parliament. It is not good enough for us to give a rubber stamp approval to these private companies. If there is any reason for their wishing to be incorporated by parliament, then there is a justification for giving greater attention to these bills. I am certainly not suggesting that the sponsor of the bill has not considered this matter sufficiently because I am sure he has, in view of the fact that the people he represents will be the ones who will really suffer if we do not handle the granting of these licences so as to protect the people who will invest in these companies, who will work in these fields in an atmosphere of exhilaration and who may find themselves in a sad state if the companies are not successful in their operations.
Another consideration must be taken into account so far as the National Energy Board is concerned, and that is the fact that we are importing into Canada more oil than we are exporting. Surely the National Energy Board should consider that. In view of this, perhaps we should consider the construction of an east-west pipe line which would handle enough crude to supply the needs of the eastern markets, rather than import crude from Venezuela. If this is not feasible, then perhaps we should make an arrangement with the United States to bring in oil where it is easier and to return it from another area from which it can be supplied easier. We should consider some such arrangement, rather than the haphazard one which the National Energy Board seems to be planning. If this were done we may find it preferable not to grant further drilling permits in the Northwest Territories at this time, because I anticipate that vast quantities of oil will be discovered in that area. We may then find ourselves in a situation similar to that of Elliot Lake, where a large development took place and a great outlay of capital was made, following which there was no longer a market for the product.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
Who suffers? The company does not suffer because it has a tax exemption over a long period of time. The shareholders do not suffer because they will be able to liquidate their holdings long before the man who has a house

January 30, 1968
Private Bills
in the new community which is dependent upon this resource. For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I would entreat the hon. member for Northwest Territories to refer this bill back to the standing committee so we can have a look at it. I am not so sure we were right in passing the last bill, since 1 have found certain implications in it which I did not realize were there. We made representations, and those representations were met. I think we have some responsibility in the matter. Now that I have pursued the matter further and in greater depth, I feel the member has a responsibility to investigate the potential for exploitation that will obviously prevail with the granting of an interprovincial licence, which will allow this company to move from Alberta. I am sure everyone will agree there has been a great deal of exploitation in Alberta. This province does not seem to mind as long as you pay for it. We may find that the Northwest Territories cannot be compensated in a way that will produce anything for the people or for the rest of Canada.
Before I resume my seat, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that if some of these things are not clarified in the bill, and some of the junk removed, then I feel this will indicate the company does not want to proceed with the bill. I will consider it in that light.

While other members were speaking, Mr. Chairman, I reviewed the debate on this particular bill and I noted it received considerable attention on two occasions, last June and again in November. It is now before parliament for the fourth time and does not have much prospect of being passed. From time to time we hear complaints from people about parliament being very slow in passing certain legislation. I have on occasions wondered about so many of the private bills which appear to stand on the order paper for a considerable length of time. It seems to me that sponsors of bills of this nature should pay closer attention to the operations of parliament.
As I read over the earlier debates I found, and I may have missed a few names, that the hon. members for Acadia, Kindersley, Edmonton West, Calgary South, Timiskaming, Skeena and Comox-Alberni have all had useful and appropriate remarks to make with regard to this particular bill. Despite this, the bill has not been modified. We have not heard from the sponsor as to whether it is going to be modified in accordance with the suggestions made by these members, and perhaps

others who may have spoken. The bill is still in the house and is being debated today. Obviously it will not go through.

This paragraph indicates that, other things being equal, from the technical standpoint or from the audience point of view, the board will have to take into consideration that the C.B.C. is a public service and the private stations are private enterprise, and that there is a difference in nature between them. If we do not give the B.B.G. this criterion, it will be a very bad service to do them.
I have often heard from professional workers in broadcasting a criticism that seems well founded to me, it is that heretofore legal texts governing broadcasting in Canada were not sufficiently explicit. Decision making cannot be left to a board of governors if the legislator does not write into the act his own interpretation of the role the board of governors is to fulfil. If the government fails to indicate in what direction the rules must be made, the men appointed to the board are left in doubt and uncertainty and they are put in a most difficult situation because we ourselves as legislators have failed to take our responsibilities.
Why must we supply this standard of judgment and indicate to the authorities who will be intrusted with making the rules in what direction parliament wants those decisions to be made? As I said, there is a difference in nature between the crown corporation and the private sector.

I listened carefully to the remarks of the minister this afternoon, in which she endeavoured to establish that what is really involved here is not an interest against an interest, but rather an objective set by parliament on the one hand in respect of a public interest and on the other a private interest. I wish I could agree with the hon. lady because I would then have no difficulty at all in accepting her view and supporting the subclause without amendment. But I cannot accept her view as to how the word "objective" will be interpreted, and I regret I have to reject her argument. Therefore I support the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg South.
I have some examples I should like to cite in support of my contention that the minister's interpretation is simply not applicable. If one looks at a dictionary, and I believe in fact my colleague the hon. member for Halifax has done so, one will find that the dictionary definition differs as between the interpretation of the words "objective" and "interest". That is all very well, but when busy members of a board are interpreting an objective they are not going to look up the dictionary definition. If they do they will be argued out of their position by the practical situation of the moment.
I am quite satisfied that if the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has an interest in reserving a position for a station in any particular city, it will readily make an interpretation to the Board of Broadcast Governors, or the new radio-television council, to the effect that this is in the interests of or in accord with the objectives of the Canadian

Broadcasting Corporation. I am sure they will say that in order to achieve our great national objectives it is necessary that this reservation be maintained, and that it is necessary as an objective of the national broadcasting service that the second outlet in city "x" be reserved for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and not given to a private broadcasting interest.
On this basis, they will maintain, we have a conflict between the objectives of the national broadcasting service on the one hand and the interests of some private station on the other, and it must be resolved in favour of the public system. This is nonsense. I submit, with respect, that it is nonsense to suppose that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will be able to maintain that nice distinction between this interest on the one hand and the objectives of a national broadcasting service on the other.
I should like to give an example, which astounded me, in respect of the practical application of this situation. In my own city of Kamloops there has been for some time an interest in the establishment of a second AM-FM radio station outlet. The application was submitted to the Board of Broadcast Governors for approval. Recently I was asked to take the matter up with the board, and I have done so. I have been informed that the applicant is aware of the policy, announced some time ago, to refrain from recommending favourably on licences for additional radio stations in markets, in which we are seeking to introduce alternative television. It so happens that the only T.V. station in Kamloops is a private station, although it is a C.B.C. affiliate. As far as I can gather, the board is concerned and interested to see that there is an extension of C.B.C coverage in Kamloops. That is a very proper interest and the people there will be happy, although this is a separate matter.
In this case we have a situation in respect of which the C.B.C. will argue that because it is in their interest to have a second C.B.C. television outlet there, the board should not allow the establishment of a second radio outlet. Could anything be more ridiculous than that the citizens of the Kamloops area should be deprived of the opportunity of a second radio outlet because somebody at an obscure height has set a policy that the board will not allow a second radio outlet until a second television outlet has been established?

At this moment I do not suggest this is C.B.C. policy, or a policy imposed by the C.B.C. on the board, but I do give this as an example of the kind of ridiculous situation we will have if an act of this parliament suggests that when there is a conflict, the conflict will always be resolved in favour of the public agency.
For these reasons I cannot see any real or cogent argument against the proposition incorporated in the amendment submitted by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg South. That amendment suggests that where there is a conflict in any area, the conflict will be resolved in favour of the public interest. It suggests that the public interest must prevail. I hope very much that a direction is adopted which is as simple as that, and that such direction be incorporated in the act. That is what this amendment would do. The Board of Broadcast Governors or the new radio and television council would then have a very simple directive.
What is the public interest in the city of Kamloops and area? That is the question the board, with this directive, would ask itself.
