Mr. Chairman, clause 2 On) deals with the conflicts that could arise between the objectives of the national broadcasting service and those of the private broadcasting service. Therefore, we are talking about conflicts.
One thing is missing in that subclause. Should a conflict arise between the national broadcasting service and the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh)-who is responsible to the house for the management of the C.B.C.-who will settle the matter? If the minister charges that the C.B.C. is rotten and the management says that it is not so, who will decide where the rottenness is? There is nothing in that subclause which states what objectives and interests will prevail should such a conflict arise.
Recently, more conflicts arose between the C.B.C. and the Secretary of State than between the private sector and the corporation. We made no special provision at that time, but I should like to know whether the Secretary of State intends to include an amendment in subclause (h) providing for the creation of a body who would settle such conflicts. In the case of a conflict as the one I just mentioned, should the Secretary of State's interests prevail over those of the C.B.C., or should it be otherwise?
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
Hon. members will recall that the minister charged the C.B.C. with rotten management. There is no provision as to the way of solving this conflict.
Some machinery should be provided for the settlement of those conflicts, because doubts exist as to charges put forward by the minister against the C.B.C.
I wonder if it would not be advisable to include some provision in the bill. I see that the parliamentary secretary is motioning to me that it is useless to do so. Nevertherless, he knows quite well that conflicts are not restricted to private and public sectors. Why always leave the Canadian people doubtful? Canadians are now wondering where is the rot. The minister cannot say yes or no, because there is no provision, no machinery to settle the differences and the question, to wit: where and at what level is the rot.
I am therefore wondering whether we should not add to subclause (h) a provision, capable of anticipating any conflict liable to arise between the hon. Secretary of State and the C.B.C. I think it is important to prevent any recurrence of those disgraceful scenes which we have been witnessing recently, and it is imperative to try and find a way to settle them once and for all.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I shall take only a minute or two to add a few comments to what has been said. I must admit that I agree entirely with my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings. I wish to speak on a rather technical point. Subclauses (d) and (g) set out in very broad general terms the objectives of the public broadcasting system. It seems to me that it will be impossible for the commission to make a decision in individual cases based upon these general objectives when we say, for example, in subclause (g) that the national broadcasting service should be a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment for people of different ages, interests and tastes covering the whole range of programming in fair proportion. That wording is so broad that I believe it would make it impossible for a specific decision to be made in any case. In other words, how could the commission ever say that it had made its decision on the two conflicting points of view of the national broadcasting service and the interests of private broadcasting?
January 30, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
I say that these words are so vague that they would not enable one to come to a fair conclusion. Therefore I believe the commission would have an impossible task in endeavouring to reach its decision on the objectives. This would seem to be a situation where we have nothing against nothing, when we attempt to reach a decision under subclause (h). In that case I can hardly see how the decision could be based on the objectives of the national broadcasting system, until these are spelled out. Obviously they will have to be spelled out in detail by the national broadcasting system. Therefore the broadcasting system will go before the board and say that in conformity with their general approach to a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment they feel that a certain situation must apply. If we should find that this is part of our objective and that this is the way it is applied, how could others hold a contrary view because they reached their decision under the umbrella of subclauses (d) and (g)?
Subclauses (d) and (g) were designed to express as clearly as possible what the objectives are, but they certainly were never set up to spell out particular cases or to give anyone the ability to say what is meant in a particular case. Surely subclauses (d) and (g) are very much like a statute which would say that the public broadcasting system may enact regulations, which regulations would spell out exactly what is meant. So in this case we have the ability of the national broadcasting service to spell out by regulation the case it is trying to put before the commission. I believe it would be an impossible and unfair task for the commission to attempt to make anything out of subclauses (d) and (g) in respect of a specific case, if the broadcasting system claimed that it was in the national interest.
Having reached this conclusion, it would be difficult for one to accept subclause (h) as it stands as representing the objectives of the national broadcasting service which should prevail, because there really is nothing on which to base a decision. Surely the national interests should prevail in such a case. I believe that in defining this one must take into consideration not only subclauses (d) and (g) but the whole situation. I think the subclause as it stands would permit an impossible situation. It would permit the national broadcasting service to declare its own objectives specifically, and therefore hamper any independent decision by the commission.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has identified a very important ingredient in this debate. He has isolated an element which some of us have been groping for and which some members farther to the left in this chamber believe has already been identified in the wording of the legislation as it potentially stands. The element to which I refer is the definition of the objectives of the national broadcasting service.
I cannot subscribe to the argument of the hon. member for York South, so far as the objectives of the national broadcasting service are concerned. I do not believe that the legislation as presently worded defines the objectives of the national broadcasting service. If it is our intention to isolate and articulate the objectives of the national broadcasting system, why do we not say so? We do not say so here. We say that there are several things the national broadcasting service should do. One is that it should constitute a balanced service of information; another is that it should be extended to all parts of Canada; another is that it should be in English and French and should contribute to a continued expression of Canadian identity.
I subscribe with the utmost enthusiasm to all these things, but this does not cover the whole area of philosophical thought, national preoccupation or the direction in which this country is moving in the whole area of broadcasting or in the area of creative or industrial activity.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
This isolates four points in respect of which there should be guide lines for services performed by the C.B.C. These should be adhered to as principles, philosophies and means. Do these cover the application of national objectivity? Of course they do not. I can think of other areas of objectivity for the guidance of the C.B.C., or any other national broadcasting system. These are not covered by the wording of subclause (g). Subclause (g) does not purport to set out these objectives. It simply identifies four things that a national broadcasting system should either be or constitute. These are entirely acceptable to everyone in this chamber. No one is more enthusiastic about the provisions of that subclause than I am, but that does not mean they cover the whole realm of possibility so far as national broadcasting service is concerned. For these reasons I suggest the argument of the hon. member for York South is specious. I
January 30, 1968

think he has conveniently and intelligently evaded and avoided the point at issue here.
What we are talking about is the letter of the law. This is something we hear a great deal about in terms of our society, our legal system and our jurisprudence. The letter of the law is that when such and such a conflict arises, for time immemorial and from this day forward, the objective of a national service shall prevail. No matter what interpretation the hon. lady places on this; no matter what philosophy hon. members contrive to purport, and no matter what objectives members of the N.D.P. want to suggest, the fact is we are talking about the letter of the law. No matter what aspect arises in respect of a dispute regarding this whole matter, the main point of the debate on subclause (g), is that the authorities should follow the guide lines imposed by this parliament.
It may well be that someone will ask why they should.
And why should they?

That is a very good question, and I should like to reply. Let me suggest to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that we are talking about a hypothetical idealistic situation which cannot exist. It is unrealistic to expect that in four or five years from now, when two litigants to a broadcasting dispute come before whatever authority might be in existence, the authority will be acquainted with the various aspects and convolutions of this debate, and the debate in committee before the legislation reached this stage. They are not going to be aware of the different philosophical approaches adopted during this debate, but they should not be deprived of the varying aspects of those approaches.
Earlier, the minister, when making a representation to my colleague the hon. member for Kamloops, asked if that member did not think the B.B.G. representatives who have sat in the gallery throughout this debate would get the point that we in the opposition are trying to make in the interest of the public. I think that was the substance of her question. This question begs the greater question namely, are we talking about the letter of the law? It does not really matter whether the representatives of the B.B.G. understand what we are talking about, but it does matter that future representatives of that body have guide lines based on our approach.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Does he propose to impose
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting on my generosity any further by asking to stand other clauses in order that he may be in the house to occupy our time during the consideration of this bill?

Let me just say in answer that if in the course of the examination of any legislation introduced by the hon. lady or any other minister we find a clause, subclause or paragraph in respect of which there is a vital interest at stake to my constituents or Canadians in general, I hope that we will be able to examine it to the fullest, and that no arbitrary or cursory rule will shut off such examination.
I suggest that you should be here in the future when these things are considered.

As I said earlier today, I appreciate the indulgence the minister has shown me in respect of this particular subclause. I have made it clear that this is one part of the bill which disturbs me greatly. The minister must concede that a great number of members in this chamber, including some of her own colleagues, are also disturbed. I do not think we have resolved this point.

If you sit down we will do
so by a vote.

I will sit down when I have completed what I have to say. I should like to make reference to what the minister proposed earlier in the day, which could be termed a sort of amendment to the amendment, or a proposal to a change. I am sure the amendment originally moved is not acceptable to many members on this side. It imposes restrictions and constrictions such as those already contained in subclause (h). It would result in a disadvantage to private enterprise in this country to a more severe extent than the subclause as it now stands. I do not find the suggestion of the minister acceptable.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock.
Progress reported.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask whether we may assume that there is no change in the business of the house and that it is the intention to continue with this bill until it is concluded?

VOCATIONAL AND TECHNICAL TRAINING- PROTEST BY STUDENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1960 a vocational and technical training act was approved by parliament to make up for the tragic gap in our educational facilities that had existed far too long. It was a great success, as has been witnessed by many, including the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) who in a recent speech made the statement that during the last three months of 1966 and early in 1967, the monthly enrolment in these schools doubled compared to last year. Then he went on to say that such success, impressive as it might be, is not enough.
Unfortunately, the present government was not satisfied with this success and they brought in a new act on April 1, 1967. Since that time our technical training program has been in serious difficulty right across the country. It is not necessary for me, nor is there time, to recite all the difficulties, but they include the problem of drop-outs, which is one of our major educational problems; and the schools, notwithstanding the rising rate of unemployment, are only half full. In addition, the program costs more, which is mainly due to increasing administrative costs. The able bodied, who formerly were able to undergo technical retraining, are now back on the relief rolls. Students who took an upgrading course last year find they are not eligible this year for continued subsistence under the O.T.A. allowances program.
The real reason for the difficulty has been the failure of the federal government to consult with the provinces. In an attempt to get to the bottom of these problems I have found that even though the act was passed by this house last April, no agreement was put before the provinces until May, after the act was actually passed. I found, too, that the manpower department had bought more space than they were able to use, with the result that the program is not fulfilling the need, as I have indicated.
The specific problem to which I should like to refer tonight arises from a protest that arose during the Christmas period in the Manitoba technical school-

maintopic: INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS AND DISPUTES INVESTIGATION ACT-INQUIRY CONCERNING STATEMENT BY ASSISTANT DEPUTY MINISTER
INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS AND DISPUTES INVESTIGATION ACT-INQUIRY CONCERNING STATEMENT BY ASSISTANT DEPUTY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this month the Labour Gazette published an article which has caused considerable but perhaps quiet excitement in some corners of the country, due to the fact that on a rare occasion in its history it published in toto the speech of an official of the Department of Labour, the highly respected Bernard Wilson, the assistant deputy minister (labour relations) of the Department of Labour. This was a speech he gave to a panel of the Canadian Association of Administrators of Labour Legislation at its twenty sixth annual conference in Ottawa, held last September. Perhaps there is nothing in the introduction to that speech which would generate special excitement, but at the end of his speech the assistant deputy minister made the following suggestion which is to be found at page 13 of that issue of the Labour Gazette:
The following extra provision, added to existing federal or provincial labour legislation, might be considered in seeking less labour unrest while giving recognition to rights that a large part of labour consider fundamental.
Notwithstanding the provisions of sections 21 and 22 of this act (the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act), where a strike or lockout has taken place and has been in effect for 14 days from the date of its inception, the governor in council may, if the strike or lockout imperils the safety or security of Canada or the economic welfare and livelihood of great numbers of its citizens, other than those participating directly in the strike or lockout, promulgate regulations for the resumption of operations by the employer and by the employees, and for the final settlement of the dispute without further strike or lockout.
To forestall the inevitable objection that the government will be brought into every important dispute in essential industry, it should be pointed out that that situation exists now. In further
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion extenuation, it can also be argued that, where great questions of public interest, critical national or regional economic loss and the exercise of human rights are concerned, there are few matters of more importance to governments, and more deserving of their time.
Indeed, the gentleman is right; this is one of the big issues of our time, namely how far the government interferes or intervenes in questions of disputes. I checked the latest speech of my friend from the Dalhousie University law school, the Minister of Labour, delivered to the University of Western Ontario law forum on January 27 and found that his position does not come up to that of Mr. Wilson.
On that occasion he said:
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The government's role surely should be a conciliatory and a mediatory one, a role that will bring the disputants together and encourage them to find a formula for settlement less costly to their immediate and separate interest than the continuation of their rigid positions would be.
In essence then, the optimum role and the responsibility of government is to continue to hold available to disputants suitable procedural machinery to enable them to find their own solutions within a reasonable period of time.
Later on in that same speech, the minister had this to say:
Because a whole new range of puzzling problems is arising in industrial relations today, I visualize -and have been planning for-a new role for my department. No longer shall we be merely the referees: now we are taking and will continue to take anticipatory initiatives. Since the very existence of our conciliation branch presupposes a possible breakdown of collective bargaining, I would view it as the greatest achievement of a Minister of Labour to make it an unnecessary part of what is now my department.
Our emphasis should-and I hope will-change to becoming a trusted and "honest broker" before real trouble breaks out. We should become fire prevention officers, not firefighters.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think there is probably enough difference in these points of view to indicate that this is a matter of some considerable public concern, and something which will be debated in Canada no doubt over the next five or ten years. In view of this fact, I thought I would pose a question to the minister to see if his philosophy leans one way or the other or whether Mr. Bernard Wilson was merely floating a very large balloon, the largest balloon I have seen floated by a civil servant in Canada. I am endeavouring to ascertain whether Mr. Wilson was expressing something which will eventually become government policy.
January 30, 1968

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS AND DISPUTES INVESTIGATION ACT-INQUIRY CONCERNING STATEMENT BY ASSISTANT DEPUTY MINISTER
speechtext:
When the question was put a few days ago by my hon. friend, I thought my parliamentary secretary gave a very good answer. He said emphatically and unequivocally that no legislation such as that suggested in the question was in contemplation. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, a word of explanation as to how the article came to be published would be of interest. There is an organization in Canada known as the Canadian Association of Administrators of Labour Legislation. The membership consists of the federal deputy minister and the ten provincial deputy ministers of labour. They, and their senior officials, meet annually to discuss matters or to think out loud about what may or may not be done to improve labour-management relations in this country.
Last year's meeting that took place in Ottawa in September last was the one in which the assistant deputy minister, to whom reference has been made by my hon. friend put forward as a suggestion the one referred to by my hon. friend, amongst a number of other suggestions. It so happens one of the western provinces, Alberta I think, has legislation similar to that which was suggested as something that might be considered by the group attending this conference. The suggestion was put forward merely as something that might be considered by those in attendance. There are a number of other suggestions in the paper.
One of those suggestions was that the right to strike might even be extended on certain occasions rather than curtailed, which is the exact antithesis of what was covered in the question raised by my hon. friend. I assure my hon. friend and others that these meetings which are held regularly, and I have been following them now for over two years, are really worth while. They are stimulating. This provocative paper which was presented by the assistant deputy minister was one of several put forward to provoke discussion. I wish we had a lot more discussions of that kind. The paper was so good the editor of the Labour Review published the article almost in toto. Therein lies the explanation for the article and how it came to be published.
